title: RBI Holds Rates and Raises Growth Forecast as Iran War Shock Eases
excerpt: India's central bank raised its growth projection to 6.7% and lowered inflation forecasts, diverging from global peers racing to hike rates in response to the Iran conflict.
body:
• The RBI kept its repo rate unchanged at 5.25% for the third consecutive meeting, with a unanimous vote to maintain a neutral stance despite inflation crossing its 4% target.
  • Growth forecast raised to 6.7% and inflation projection lowered to 5% for the current fiscal year, signaling the central bank believes the worst of the Iran war's economic shock has passed.
  • Special measures to attract dollar inflows — including scrapping capital gains tax for foreign government bond holders — have pulled in nearly $40 billion, stabilizing the rupee after a 7% decline this year.

The Reserve Bank of India kept interest rates unchanged on August 5 and offered a more optimistic economic outlook, signaling that the worst of the initial shock from the Iran conflict may be fading even as the war continues to roil global energy markets.

Governor Sanjay Malhotra announced that the six-member Monetary Policy Committee voted unanimously to hold the repo rate at 5.25% and maintain a neutral stance — the third consecutive pause since the central bank cut rates by 25 basis points in December.

A Brighter Forecast

In a notable shift, the RBI raised its GDP growth projection for the current fiscal year to 6.7%, up from its earlier estimate, while lowering the inflation forecast to 5%. The revised numbers suggest the central bank believes India's economy is absorbing the oil price shock better than initially feared.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=GjbxmRSRQs0

Retail inflation rose to 4.38% in June — the first reading above the RBI's 4% medium-term target in 17 months — but remained well within the 2% to 6% tolerance band. Core inflation, which strips out volatile food and fuel prices, held near 4%.

"Although core and underlying inflation have risen modestly, they remain within the RBI's comfort zone. Consequently, a rate hike is unlikely in 2026 unless core inflation sustains above 4.5%."

— Samiran Chakraborty, Chief India Economist, Citi

Holding the Line While Peers Hike

The RBI's decision to stand pat sets it apart from a growing list of central banks that have raised borrowing costs since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran erupted five months ago. Central banks in Europe, Australia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore, South Korea, and South Africa have all hiked rates. The Federal Reserve and Bank of Japan have held steady.

Malhotra called discussions of a rate hike "premature," a view that prompted economists to scale back expectations. A July Reuters poll found 68 of 72 respondents expected no change in August, and poll medians now show rates on hold at least through early 2027.

"We have already seen some of the effects of the war trickle down to inflation, but it will be too quick a reaction by the central bank to hike rates now because growth will be affected adversely," said Aditya Vyas, chief economist at STCI Primary Dealer.

Dollar Inflows Shore Up the Rupee

Instead of raising rates to defend the currency, the RBI deployed a series of measures to attract foreign capital. In June, it scrapped capital gains tax for foreign holders of Indian government bonds and sweetened dollar deposit schemes for non-resident Indians. The steps have attracted nearly $40 billion in inflows, according to Reuters.

The rupee closed at 95.38 last week, posting its biggest weekly gain since March after sustained central bank interventions. But the currency remains under pressure — down roughly 7% this year and about 6% since the Iran conflict began in late February — as renewed hostilities in the Gulf have lifted oil prices again.

India imports about 90% of its oil, making it particularly vulnerable to supply disruptions. Foreign investors pulled nearly $19 billion from Indian markets between March and April, contributing to the rupee's slide to record lows.

What Comes Next

Interest-rate swap markets are pricing in roughly 75 basis points of hikes over the next 12 months, reflecting the gap between the RBI's patience and the market's expectations. Goldman Sachs expects the central bank to raise rates by 25 basis points each in October and December.

"If you compare India to similarly rated markets, it's not the most compelling story from a real yields perspective. Fundamentally, I think the right call for India is higher rates. They are not going to do it this week but the longer they wait, the more they will be pushed to it."

— Trinh Nguyen, Senior Economist for Emerging Asia, Natixis

The RBI's latest Financial Stability Report, released in late June, offered further reason for its measured approach. It showed Indian banks' gross bad loan ratio at 1.8% — projected to remain below 2% through March 2028 — and described the financial system as "remarkably resilient despite facing external shocks of significant magnitude."

Whether the central bank can maintain its hold-and-wait strategy depends largely on the trajectory of the war, the monsoon season's impact on food prices, and how quickly wholesale price pressures — at 9.87% in June — feed through to consumer prices.
